```{r setup, include = FALSE}
                      fig.height = 4, dpi = 80)
library(hyperutils)
```

Every analysis starts with a data frame. This vignette shows how to read the
files that clinical pharmacology data usually come in, how to derive and
recode columns, how to filter rows safely and how to build a clean analysis
dataset in one documented call.

## The dataset conventions

The functions of the package assume the NONMEM-style layout that most
pharmacometric work uses: one row per dose or observation, one subject after
the other, with the columns

| Column | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| `ID` | subject identifier |
| `TIME` | time of the record, for example hours since the first dose |
| `DV` | observed value (concentration or response) |
| `AMT` | dose amount, 0 or missing on observation rows |
| `EVID` | event type: 0 observation, 1 dose, 4 reset and dose |
| `MDV` | 1 when `DV` must not be used |
| `CMT`, `DVID` | compartment and the type of the observation |
| `ADDL`, `II`, `SS`, `RATE` | additional doses, interdose interval, steady-state flag, infusion rate |

Your column names may differ. Every function that needs one of them has an
argument to name it, for example `hp_nca(d, id = "SUBJ", time = "HOURS")`.

## Reading a file

`hp_read_data()` reads comma, tab, semicolon or white-space delimited files.
It finds the delimiter itself, turns `.` into a missing value, drops comment
rows and upper-cases the column names so that later code can rely on them.

```{r read-example}
d <- hp_read_data(hp_example_file())
str(d)
```

A semicolon file with a title line and lower-case names:

```{r read-odd}
tmp <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
writeLines(c("Study XYZ-001",
             "id;time;dv;wt",
             "1;0;.;70.5",
             "1;1;4.2;70.5",
             "1;2;3.1;70.5"), tmp)
hp_read_data(tmp, skip = 1)
```

Keep the column names as written with `upper = FALSE`, change the missing
value codes with `na.strings`, and force the delimiter with `delimiter` if
the guess is wrong:

```{r read-options}
hp_read_data(tmp, skip = 1, upper = FALSE)
unlink(tmp)
```

### NONMEM table files

A NONMEM `$TABLE` output has a `TABLE NO. 1` line and repeats its header.
`hp_read_data()` removes those lines, and when the file holds several tables
it adds a `TABLE_NO` column:

```{r nonmem-table}
tmp <- tempfile(fileext = ".tab")
writeLines(c("TABLE NO.     1",
             " ID TIME DV PRED",
             " 1 0 0 0",
             " 1 1 2.5 2.4",
             "TABLE NO.     2",
             " ID TIME DV PRED",
             " 2 0 0 0",
             " 2 1 3.1 2.9"), tmp)
hp_read_data(tmp)
unlink(tmp)
```

## Deriving columns with `hp_mutate()`

`hp_mutate()` runs statements written as text, in order. A later statement can
use a column made by an earlier one. Text statements are convenient because
the same text can be stored in a settings file, a log or a script header.

```{r mutate}
d2 <- hp_mutate(d, c(
  "LNDV = log(DV)",
  "BSA = 0.007184 * WT^0.425 * 170^0.725",
  "WTGRP = case_when(WT < 70 ~ 'light', WT < 85 ~ 'medium', TRUE ~ 'heavy')",
  "MALE = ifelse(SEX == 1, 'male', 'female')"
))
head(d2[d2$EVID == 0, c("ID", "TIME", "DV", "LNDV", "BSA", "WTGRP", "MALE")], 4)
```

Two things to know:

* `case_when()` evaluates the pairs in order and uses the first test that is
  true. End with `TRUE ~ value` to give every other row a value; without it
  they become `NA`.
* A statement that fails stops with a message that names it, so a typo does
  not silently produce a column of missing values.

```{r mutate-error, error = TRUE}
hp_mutate(d, "BAD = log(NOTACOLUMN)")
```

## Filtering rows with `hp_filter()`

`hp_filter()` keeps the rows for which a condition is true. It differs from
`subset()` in one way that matters for clinical data: a row whose test is
`NA` is dropped, never kept.

```{r filter}
nrow(d)
nrow(hp_filter(d, "EVID == 0"))
nrow(hp_filter(d, "EVID == 0 & WT > 80 & DOSEGRP == 200"))
```

The same expression text works as the `filter` argument of `hp_nca()`,
`hp_nca_read()` and `hp_eda_prepare()`, and as the `obs_filter` argument that
removes observations while keeping all dose records.

## One call for the whole analysis dataset

`hp_custom_prep()` chains the steps in a fixed order: mutate, filter,
distinct, sort, head, select. Fixing the order makes the call easy to read
and to review.

```{r prep}
# one row per subject with a derived exposure group
subj <- hp_custom_prep(
  d,
  filter   = "EVID == 1",
  mutate   = "DOSEMG = AMT; HIGH = AMT >= 200",
  distinct = "ID",
  select   = c("ID", "DOSEMG", "HIGH", "WT", "AGE", "SEX")
)
head(subj)
```

```{r prep-sort}
# the five highest observed concentrations
hp_custom_prep(d, filter = "EVID == 0", sort = "-DV", head = 5,
               select = c("ID", "TIME", "DV"))
```

A leading minus in `sort` sorts downwards.

## Descriptive statistics

`hp_describe()` returns the statistics of a clinical pharmacology summary in
one call.

```{r describe}
round(hp_describe(subj$WT), 2)
```

Use `sapply()` over a split to get them by group:

```{r describe-groups}
sapply(split(subj$WT, subj$HIGH), function(v) hp_describe(v)[c("n", "mean", "sd", "geomean")])
```

## Checking the data before analysis

A short checklist that avoids most problems later:

1. `str(d)`: are the numeric columns numeric? A text column that should be
   numeric usually contains a stray character.
2. `table(d$EVID)` and `sum(d$AMT > 0, na.rm = TRUE)`: are there dose records?
3. `tapply(d$TIME, d$ID, min)`: does every subject start at or after the
   first dose?
4. `hp_eda_missing(hp_eda_prepare(d))`: which columns have missing values
   (see `vignette("exploratory-analysis")`)?
5. Samples that are 0 or below the limit of quantification: decide on a BLQ
   rule before you analyse (see `vignette("nca-step-by-step")`).
